facts.claim: Greek Law 5089/2024 is titled 'Equality in civil marriage, amendment of the Civil Code and other provisions' (in Greek: 'Isotita ston politiko gamo'). It was published in the Government Gazette (FEK) A' 27 on 16 February 2024 (text as reproduced by e-EFKA, a Greek government agency; original Greek, translated here).
Article 15 of Law 5089/2024 states that the law comes into force from its publication in the Government Gazette (16 February 2024), unless otherwise provided in individual provisions.
The Hellenic Parliament's legislative record for Law 5089 shows the bill was tabled on 01/02/2024 by the Ministry of State, voted on 15/02/2024, and published as FEK 27 A'/16.2.2024.

Article 1 of Law 5089/2024 states its purpose is to secure the principle of equality by extending the possibility of marriage to persons of the same sex, and to strengthen protection from discrimination, towards implementing the National Strategy for LGBTQI Equality.

Article 3 of Law 5089/2024 amends article 1350(1) of the Greek Civil Code to read: 'Marriage is contracted between two persons of different or the same sex. Marriage requires the agreement of the intending spouses. The relevant declarations are made in person and without condition or time limit.' (translated from Greek)

Ministry of Interior Circular 240 (4 March 2024), sent to all municipalities, registry offices and Greek consular authorities, states that following Law 5089/2024 a marriage between two persons of the same sex is considered valid in the Greek legal order, is registered in the civil registry books and recorded in the Citizens' Register (Mitroo Politon). It also notes that new templates for the declaration of a civil marriage were posted on the Ministry of Interior website.

Circular 240 states that, per the law's explanatory report, the law does not interfere with the constitutionally protected freedom of the Eastern Orthodox Church or other religions known in Greece (article 1367 Civil Code) to set the conditions of a religious ceremony. In other words, the reform is to civil marriage; it does not oblige any church to perform a same-sex religious wedding.
Circular 240 states that the law does not amend the Civil Code provisions on medically assisted reproduction (articles 1455 to 1460), which remain as they are.

Circular 240 states the law does not amend the adoption articles (1542 onwards) but that extending marriage to same-sex couples means the adoption provisions apply to them, including adoption of a minor by a same-sex couple and adoption of one spouse's child by the other; a child gains a legal family tie to the parent's same-sex spouse only if adopted by them.

Article 10 of Law 5089/2024 recognises as valid, from the date they took place, same-sex marriages of Greek citizens performed abroad before the law came into force under the law of the place of celebration, unless one spouse has since entered a new valid marriage, the marriage's non-existence was already recognised by an irrevocable Greek court decision, or the marriage was dissolved or annulled. Circular 240 notes this concerns marriages where at least one spouse is a Greek citizen.

Article 11 of Law 5089/2024 provides that a parent-child relationship recorded in public documents or a court decision of a third country is recognised in Greece regardless of the sex of one or both parents.

Article 13 of Law 5089/2024 allowed same-sex couples in a Greek cohabitation agreement (Law 4356/2015) to marry within one year of the law coming into force and declare that the marriage applies retrospectively from the date of the cohabitation agreement. This was a one-year transitional window from 16 February 2024.

Article 4 of Law 5089/2024 amends article 1505 Civil Code: if parents do not declare their children's surname, children take a compound surname of both parents' surnames, the alphabetically first placed first; the surname declaration is made before the marriage, to a notary or to the officiant, who must request it. This applies to marriages performed after the law came into force.

Law 5089/2024 (articles 6 to 8) extends parental leave, maternity-related benefits and other spousal and parental entitlements under Greek employment and social security law to same-sex spouses and parents.

Neither the text of Law 5089/2024 nor Ministry of Interior Circular 240 (as read) states any Greek residency or Greek nationality requirement for a same-sex couple to marry in Greece. Article 3 simply amends the Civil Code marriage condition. Neither document addresses how foreign nationals' capacity to marry is assessed; the law's foreign-element chapter (articles 10 and 11) deals only with marriages and parentage created abroad.

[Copied from rhodes-wedding-venues fact_600] The Municipality of Rhodes (rhodes.gr) publishes a page, in Greek, listing the supporting documents for performing a civil marriage of foreign nationals (under article 5(1) of Presidential Decree 391/1982): a joint application by the couple; a marriage licence or a certificate of no impediment to marriage from the person's consular or other public authority, naming the person they will marry, valid for six months; a copy of each passport; a municipal fee (a fee applies); and a form with the newlyweds' details.

[Copied from rhodes-wedding-venues fact_601] The Municipality of Rhodes page states that documents issued by foreign authorities must be originals of recent issue and officially translated into Greek, by a Greek lawyer, by the Greek Embassy abroad or by the Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and that for countries outside the European Union they require certification with the Apostille stamp.

[Copied from rhodes-wedding-venues fact_602] The Municipality of Rhodes page states that details not shown on the documents provided can be recorded after the couple files a solemn declaration under Law 1599/1986, using the municipality's template.

[Copied from rhodes-wedding-venues fact_500] The Municipality of Rhodes 'Ceremony Venues' page (rhodes.gr, page last modified January 2024) lists civil ceremony locations for Rhodes City: Square of Antinavarchou P. Ioannidi; Acropoleos Street on St Stefanos hill (Monte Smith); Rodini park including courtyard; the Rodian Mansion including courtyard (marked 'temporarily unavailable due to renovation'); the Aquarium courtyard; and the Town Hall's central entrance staircase. A Rhodes City registrar is named at Rhodes Town Hall.
facts.conflicts: The page does not list any site inside the medieval Old Town walls as a civil ceremony location. The Rodian Mansion is flagged as temporarily unavailable on a page last modified January 2024, so its current status needs checking.

facts.claim: [Copied from rhodes-wedding-venues fact_501] The same municipal page lists Filerimos as the civil ceremony location for Ialysos, and Kallithea Springs & Spa, Faliraki Beach and Koskinou Beach for Kallithea, each region with its own named registrar.

[Copied from rhodes-wedding-venues fact_502] For Lindos the municipal page lists Lindos Town Hall; St Paul's chapel / platform, described as 'perhaps the most picturesque setting of all', a tiny chapel perched below a cliff in the shadow of the Acropolis of Lindos next to the turquoise waters of St Paul's Bay; and Vliha Beach, on the seaside in front of a named hotel. Lindos has its own registrar at Lindos Town Hall.

[Copied from rhodes-wedding-venues fact_503] The municipal page also lists civil ceremony locations in the Afandou region (including Afandou beach and Kolimbia beach), Archangelos region (Stegna beach, Petronas area at Stegna, Agia Agathi beach at Malona, Haraki beach), Attaviros region (Old Town Hall of Embonas and municipal communities of Agios Isidoros, Kritinia, Monolithos and Sianna), Kameiros region (neoclassical Municipal Library of Soroni), Petaloudes region (including the Valley of Butterflies and the old windmill of Maritsa), South Rhodes (including Prasonisi, Plimmiri and the coastline of Asklipio at Kiotari) and the Elafos hotel area on Prophet Ilias, Salakos.

[Copied from rhodes-wedding-venues fact_504] Municipal conditions stated (Registry Office, Municipality of Rhodes): required documents include a full birth certificate translated into Greek, valid marriage licences or certificates of no impediment naming both partners and the wedding place, divorce or death certificates where relevant, a residence permit for non-EU countries, and passport copies; documents need an Apostille where applicable, also translated into Greek. Originals must be presented to the registrar two days before the wedding. A fee applies, payable at the registry office.
facts.conflicts: This page lists 'a residence permit for non-EU countries' and a full birth certificate, which the Greek-language documents page (fact_16) does not list. Ask the Rhodes registry which list is current for non-EU (e.g. Australian) couples.

facts.claim: [Copied from rhodes-wedding-venues fact_505] The municipal page says the Town Hall of Rhodes ceremony takes place every Wednesday and Friday, with the couple returning to the registry office the next working day to sign and have the marriage certificate drawn up, and that two adult witnesses over 18 must be present.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: weddings are performed by a Priest recognised as canonical by the Archdiocese; the laws and regulations for weddings are set by the Holy Canons of the Orthodox Church and implemented by the Archdiocese, and apply to every Greek Orthodox Priest across Australia. [Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding part-3 fact_310.]

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: the crowning is the climax of the Marriage Service; the crowns are a sign of the bond between bride and groom and represent the glory and honour God bestows on the couple. Crowns were usually plaited of lemon blossoms or flowers; today they are often silver or gold. The Best Man exchanges the crowns three times while the Priest and Chanter sing 'Lord our God, crown them in glory and honour.' [Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding part-3 fact_304.]

The Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia's marriage page (Laws & Regulations) states: 'The sacramental union of a man and a woman is performed in an Orthodox Church according to the liturgical tradition, and blessed by a Priest who is recognised as canonical (authentic) by the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia.' Its Ceremony of Marriage section says marriage is a Sacrament 'through which the union of man and woman is sanctified by God.'

insider_details.detail: Greece's same-sex marriage law is a civil marriage reform. Plan the legal ceremony with the municipality's registrar (dimarchos or registrar), and treat any religious element as symbolic, because the law expressly leaves churches free to set their own rules.

Legal paperwork, not the venue, sets the timeline. On Rhodes the certificate of no impediment must name your partner and is valid for six months, foreign documents need an Apostille and a Greek translation, and the originals go to the registrar two days before the ceremony. Build at least a week on the island before the wedding date so nothing is rushed.

On Rhodes the municipal civil ceremony can be held well beyond the Town Hall: Lindos' St Paul's chapel platform, Kallithea Springs, Filerimos and a list of beaches are all named municipal ceremony locations, each served by a local registrar. Choose the registrar region first, then the venue.

Rhodes Town Hall ceremonies run on Wednesdays and Fridays, and the couple goes back to the registry the next working day to sign and have the marriage certificate drawn up. Avoid booking a departure flight for the morning after.

If either partner has a child, the law's surname rule applies: the surname declaration for future children is made before the wedding to a notary or the officiant. Raise this with your Wedded Advisor early if it matters to you.

Order the paperwork from both ends early: Smartraveller says DFAT can issue a CNI in Australia but some authorities only accept ones issued locally, and the Embassy in Athens needs an appointment (weekday mornings) for notarial work, though CNI paperwork can go by post. Ask the municipality which version it accepts before booking flights.

Once married in Greece, you can't marry each other again in Australia if the marriage is recognised, so a home celebration should be framed as a recommitment or confirmation of vows, not a second wedding.

Plan guest comfort around the island: Smartraveller says attitudes are generally more accepting on Mykonos, Santorini and Ios and advises avoiding public displays of affection in rural areas, so keep mainland or village excursions in mind when planning the welcome and farewell events.

Brief the wedding party on safety without alarm: Smartraveller notes homophobic attacks and drink spiking have occurred, including on the main islands, so organise transfers back to the hotel after the reception rather than leaving guests to find late-night taxis.

Check passports for every guest: Smartraveller warns that an 'X' sex marker can't be guaranteed for entry or transit, and the EES border registration can cause queues, so guests should check transit countries and allow extra time on arrival.
